title: Femoral triangle (anterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender, with surface detail added by an image model.

rows: Anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. It is the rolled-under lower edge of the aponeurosis of the external oblique.
Forms the floor of the inguinal canal. The femoral nerve, artery, and vein and the iliopsoas pass under it into the thigh.
hy: It is the base of the femoral triangle. Sartorius is the lateral border and adductor longus the medial border. Under the ligament, from lateral to medial, lie the femoral nerve, artery, and vein and then the lymphatics (NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics).
A hernia that comes out above the ligament is inguinal. One that comes out below it, through the femoral canal, is femoral.

rows: Upper part of the medial surface of the tibia, with gracilis and semitendinosus (pes anserinus).
Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh at the hip and flexes the leg at the knee, as in sitting cross-legged.
hy: The bursa under the pes anserinus can become inflamed and cause pain on the medial side of the knee.

rows: Body of the pubis, below the pubic crest.
Middle third of the linea aspera of the femur.
Pectineal line on the superior ramus of the pubis.
Pectineal line of the femur, just below the lesser trochanter.
Femoral nerve (L2, L3), and sometimes also a branch of the obturator nerve.
Adducts and flexes the thigh at the hip.
Iliac fossa and the ala of the sacrum.
Lesser trochanter of the femur, with the tendon of psoas major.
With psoas major, flexes the thigh at the hip.
Bodies and intervertebral discs of T12 to L5 and the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae.
Lesser trochanter of the femur, by a tendon shared with iliacus.
Anterior rami of L1 to L3.
With iliacus it is the strongest flexor of the thigh at the hip. With the limb fixed it flexes the trunk on the thigh, as in sitting up.
hy: Pus under its fascia (psoas abscess, classically from tuberculosis of the spine) can track down to the groin. Pain when the hip is extended is the psoas sign, also seen when an inflamed appendix lies against the muscle.

rows: Lumbar plexus, from the posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2 to L4.

Forms inside psoas major, emerges from its lateral border, and runs down in the groove between psoas major and iliacus. It passes under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery, outside the femoral sheath, and breaks up into its branches a few centimeters below the ligament.
Muscles: iliacus, pectineus, sartorius, and quadriceps femoris. Skin: front and medial side of the thigh and, through the saphenous nerve, the medial side of the leg and foot.
hy: It can be injured by a fracture of the pelvis or pressed on by a hematoma or abscess in psoas major. Flexion of the hip and extension of the knee are weak, the knee jerk is reduced or lost, and the front of the thigh and the medial side of the leg are numb.

rows: Continues the external iliac artery behind the inguinal ligament.

Descends through the femoral triangle, with the femoral nerve on its lateral side and the femoral vein on its medial side, then through the adductor canal under sartorius. It passes through the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus and becomes the popliteal artery.
The lower limb. In the thigh its main branch is the deep femoral artery. Small branches near its start supply the lower abdominal wall and the external genitalia.
hy: The femoral pulse is felt just below the inguinal ligament, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. The artery is often entered here for catheter procedures such as coronary angiography.
From lateral to medial under the inguinal ligament: femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space (the femoral canal), Lymphatics (NAVEL).
A puncture made above the inguinal ligament can bleed into the retroperitoneal space, where the bleeding is hidden and cannot be stopped by pressing on it.

rows: Lower limb. It continues the popliteal vein at the adductor hiatus and receives the deep femoral vein and the great saphenous vein.
Runs up through the adductor canal behind the femoral artery and then through the femoral triangle on the medial side of the artery, inside the femoral sheath.
Becomes the external iliac vein behind the inguinal ligament.
hy: Deep vein thrombosis often begins in the veins of the calf. A clot that extends into the popliteal, femoral, or iliac veins can break off and travel to the lungs (pulmonary embolism).

rows: Medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, and the skin and superficial tissues of the medial side of the leg and thigh. Near its end it receives veins from the lower abdominal wall and the external genitalia.

Passes in front of the medial malleolus and runs up the medial side of the leg with the saphenous nerve. It passes behind the medial condyle of the femur, runs up the medial side of the thigh, and goes through the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
hy: Commonly removed and used as a graft in coronary artery bypass surgery. The vein is turned around so that its valves do not block the flow.
Varicose veins: when the valves of the saphenous veins and of the perforating veins fail, blood flows backward and pools, and the superficial veins become wide and twisted.

rows: Anterior superior iliac spine and the front part of the iliac crest.
Iliotibial tract, which attaches to the lateral condyle of the tibia.
Flexes, abducts, and medially rotates the thigh. Tightens the iliotibial tract, which steadies the extended knee.
Thickened lateral band of the fascia lata, from the iliac crest to the anterolateral (Gerdy) tubercle on the lateral condyle of the tibia.
Receives the insertions of tensor fasciae latae and most of gluteus maximus, and steadies the hip and the extended knee.
hy: Irritation where the tract crosses the lateral epicondyle of the femur, from friction or from compression of the tissue under it, causes pain on the outer side of the knee in runners and cyclists (iliotibial band syndrome).

rows: Anterior inferior iliac spine and the ilium just above the acetabulum.
Base of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, and through the patellar ligament the tibial tuberosity.
Extends the leg at the knee and helps flex the thigh at the hip. It is the only part of quadriceps femoris that crosses the hip.
hy: Tapping the patellar ligament makes quadriceps femoris contract: the knee jerk reflex, which tests the femoral nerve and the L2 to L4 segments, mainly L4.

rows: Greater trochanter and the lateral lip of the linea aspera of the femur.
Patella through the quadriceps tendon, and through the patellar ligament the tibial tuberosity.
Extends the leg at the knee.
Intertrochanteric line and the medial lip of the linea aspera of the femur.
Patella through the quadriceps tendon, and through the patellar ligament the tibial tuberosity.
Extends the leg at the knee. Its lowest fibers pull the patella medially and keep it in its groove.
Body and inferior ramus of the pubis.
Upper part of the medial surface of the tibia, with sartorius and semitendinosus (pes anserinus).
Adducts the thigh, flexes the leg at the knee, and helps rotate the flexed leg medially.
